decks.title: Symbols, Valency, Radicals and Formulae — Part 1: Symbols, valency and radicals
goals: Write the symbols of common elements, including those taken from Latin names, and say what a symbol stands for
Deduce the valency of an element from its hydride or from its valence electrons
Name common acid and basic radicals, state their valencies and tell simple radicals from compound radicals

slides.heading: The shorthand of chemistry
slides.body_md: Part 1 — every element has a symbol, every symbol has a combining power, and groups of atoms can behave like one unit.

visual.alt: Flow: symbol, valency, radical, formula

slides.narration: Chemists around the world write the same short signs for elements and compounds. In this lesson we build that language step by step. First the symbol, then the combining power called valency, and then radicals, which are the building blocks of compounds.

slides.heading: Symbols: a short sign for an element
slides.body_md: A **symbol** is a letter or a pair of letters that stands for an element. The first letter is a capital and the second, if any, is small.

visual.alt: Table of ten common elements and their symbols

slides.narration: A symbol is a short sign for an element. It is one capital letter, or a capital followed by a small letter. Hydrogen is H, oxygen is O, chlorine is a capital C followed by a small l, and so on. A capital second letter would be wrong, so be careful.

slides.heading: Symbols taken from Latin names
slides.body_md: Some symbols come from the **Latin** name of the element, not the English one.

visual.alt: Table of eight elements whose symbols come from Latin names

slides.narration: Many old elements were named in Latin, and their symbols still follow that name. Sodium is Na from natrium. Iron is Fe from ferrum. Silver is Ag from argentum, and gold is Au from aurum. The English name will not help you guess these, so learn the list.

slides.heading: What a symbol tells us
slides.body_md: **Qualitatively** a symbol names the element. **Quantitatively** it stands for **one atom** of the element, with its relative atomic mass.

rows: One atom of carbon, mass 12 u
One atom of magnesium, mass 24 u
One atom of sulphur, mass 32 u

visual.alt: Table giving the qualitative and quantitative meaning of three symbols

slides.narration: A symbol carries two messages. It names the element, and it stands for exactly one atom of that element, with a fixed relative mass. The symbol for magnesium means the element magnesium, and also a single atom of magnesium.

slides.heading: Quick check: symbols
slides.body_md: Match the symbol to the element.

visual.alt: Three symbols with the Latin names they come from

slides.narration: Which symbol belongs to which element? Use the Latin names to help you.

slides.heading: Valency: the combining power of an atom
slides.body_md: **Valency** is the number of hydrogen atoms (or atoms that can replace them) that one atom of an element **combines with**. Hydrogen itself has valency 1.

visual.alt: Table of four hydrides and the valency of the element in each

slides.narration: Valency tells us how many hydrogen atoms one atom can hold on to. Chlorine takes one, oxygen takes two, nitrogen takes three and carbon takes four. So their valencies are one, two, three and four.

slides.heading: Valency from the outer shell
slides.body_md: Look at the **red** electrons in the outer shell. They decide the valency.

visual.alt: Electron shells of sodium, magnesium, nitrogen and chlorine, with their valencies

slides.narration: Sodium has one electron in its outer shell and valency one. Magnesium has two outer electrons and valency two. Nitrogen has five outer electrons, so it gains three to fill the shell, and its valency is three. Chlorine has seven, needs one more, and has valency one.

slides.heading: The valence-electron rule
slides.body_md:
**Valence electrons** are the electrons in the outermost shell.

- **Metals** lose their valence electrons: valency = number of valence electrons (1, 2 or 3).
- **Non-metals** gain electrons to reach eight: valency = **8 minus** the number of valence electrons.

visual.alt: Table linking the number of valence electrons to valency from one to eight

slides.narration: If an atom has one, two or three valence electrons, that number is its valency. With four valence electrons the valency is also four. With five, six or seven, subtract from eight. A full shell of eight electrons means valency zero, as in the noble gases.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: valency from the electron arrangement
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The electron arrangements of phosphorus and sulphur are 2, 8, 5 and 2, 8, 6. Find the valency of each and classify it.

**Step 1.** Outer shell of phosphorus has 5 electrons. Atom needs 3 more, so valency $= 8 - 5 = 3$, a **trivalent** non-metal.

**Step 2.** Outer shell of sulphur has 6 electrons. Valency $= 8 - 6 = 2$, a **divalent** non-metal.

visual.alt: Table working out the valencies of phosphorus and sulphur

slides.narration: Phosphorus has five electrons in its outer shell. It is a non-metal, so we subtract from eight, and the valency is three. Sulphur has six, and eight minus six gives a valency of two. Phosphorus is trivalent and sulphur is divalent.

slides.heading: Quick check: valency
slides.body_md: Use the rule on an aluminium atom.

visual.alt: Electron arrangement of aluminium

slides.narration: Aluminium has three electrons in its outer shell. Is it a metal or a non-metal, and what is its valency?

slides.heading: Mono-, di-, tri- and tetravalent
slides.body_md: Elements are grouped by valency. Some metals show **variable valency**, shown in the name by a Roman number, as in iron(II) and iron(III).

visual.alt: Table of monovalent, divalent, trivalent and tetravalent elements with examples

slides.narration: An element is monovalent if its valency is one, divalent for two, trivalent for three and tetravalent for four. A few metals, such as iron and copper, can show more than one valency, so their names carry a number to say which one is meant.

slides.heading: Radicals: atoms that travel together
slides.body_md: A **radical** is an atom or a group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as one unit in a reaction. A **simple radical** is one atom. A **compound radical** is a group of atoms.

visual.alt: Table of simple and compound radicals, positive and negative

slides.narration: A radical is an atom or a group of atoms with a charge. A simple radical is a single atom, such as the sodium ion or the chloride ion. A compound radical is a group, such as sulphate or ammonium, and the whole group moves as one unit.

slides.heading: Common positive (basic) radicals

visual.alt: Table of common positive radicals grouped by valency

slides.narration: Learn the positive radicals by their valency. Sodium, potassium, silver and ammonium carry one positive charge. Magnesium, calcium, zinc, copper and the lower form of iron carry two. Aluminium and iron three carry three.

slides.heading: Common negative (acid) radicals

visual.alt: Table of common negative radicals grouped by valency

slides.narration: The negative radicals are grouped the same way. Chloride, nitrate, hydroxide and hydrogencarbonate each carry one negative charge. Oxide, sulphide, sulphate, carbonate and sulphite carry two. Nitride and phosphate carry three.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: valency of an acid radical
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Phosphoric acid is $\ce{H3PO4}$. Find the valency of the phosphate radical and write its charge.

**Step 1.** In water the acid gives hydrogen ions: $\ce{H3PO4 -> 3H+ + PO4^3-}$.

**Step 2.** Three hydrogen ions are released, so the radical must carry three negative charges. Valency of phosphate $= 3$.

visual.alt: Phosphoric acid giving three hydrogen ions and a phosphate radical
visual.caption: Hydrogen lost = valency of the acid radical.

slides.narration: The valency of an acid radical equals the number of hydrogen atoms the acid loses. Phosphoric acid loses three hydrogen ions, so phosphate is a trivalent negative radical.

slides.body_md: Decide whether each radical is simple or compound.

visual.alt: Three radicals with their charges

slides.narration: Which of these radicals is a compound radical, made of more than one atom?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: A symbol names an element and stands for one atom of it; some symbols come from Latin names.
Valency is the combining power; hydrogen has valency 1.
Metals: valency = valence electrons. Non-metals: valency = 8 minus valence electrons.
A radical is a charged atom or group of atoms; compound radicals move as one unit.
Valency of an acid radical = hydrogen atoms the acid loses.

rows: Group of atoms with a charge

visual.alt: Summary table of valency rules and radicals

slides.narration: To sum up. A symbol is the sign of one atom of an element. Valency comes from the outer electrons, with metals using the number as it is and non-metals subtracting from eight. A radical is a charged atom or group, and compound radicals stay together in reactions.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write symbols with a capital first letter: Co is cobalt, CO is a compound.
Learn the Latin symbols: Na, K, Fe, Cu, Ag, Au, Pb, Hg.
For non-metals use 8 minus the outer electrons.
Give the charge with the radical, not just the name.

rows: Writing CL or cl for chlorine

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: A few exam tips. Always use one capital and one small letter. Learn the Latin symbols. For non-metals, subtract the outer electrons from eight. And remember that hydroxide, sulphate, nitrate and ammonium are compound radicals.

decks.title: Symbols, Valency, Radicals and Formulae — Part 2: Formulae, names and radicals in the atmosphere
goals: Write the formula of a compound by exchanging the valencies of its radicals
Name a compound from its formula
Explain how reactive radicals in polluted air harm living things and how to reduce them

slides.heading: From valency to formula
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a formula shows which radicals are in a compound and in what numbers. The valencies tell us how to write it.

visual.alt: Flow: positive radical and negative radical, exchange valencies, formula

slides.narration: Every compound is electrically neutral. The positive charge of its radicals must cancel the negative charge. This simple idea lets us write the formula of any compound, once we know the valencies of its parts.

slides.heading: The criss-cross method
slides.body_md: The valency of one radical becomes the **subscript** of the other. Divide by a common factor if there is one, and leave out a subscript of 1.

slides.heading: Steps for writing a formula

nodes.label: Write the symbols or radicals, positive first
Write the valency of each above it
Cross the valencies over as subscripts
Divide by a common factor; drop a 1
Put a compound radical in brackets if its subscript is more than 1

visual.alt: Five steps for writing a formula from valencies

slides.narration: Five steps. Write the radicals with the positive one first. Note each valency. Cross them over. Cancel any common factor and drop a subscript of one. Finally, if a compound radical needs a subscript, put brackets around it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: aluminium sulphate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the formula of aluminium sulphate.

**Step 1.** Aluminium $\ce{Al^3+}$ has valency 3; sulphate $\ce{SO4^2-}$ has valency 2.

**Step 2.** Cross over: Al gets 2, $\ce{SO4}$ gets 3. No common factor.

**Step 3.** The sulphate is a compound radical with a subscript above 1, so it goes in brackets: **Al2(SO4)3**.

visual.alt: Table showing the criss-cross for aluminium sulphate

slides.narration: Aluminium has valency three and sulphate has valency two. Cross them over. Aluminium gets a two and sulphate gets a three. Sulphate is a group, so the three needs brackets. The formula has two aluminium atoms and three sulphate groups.

slides.heading: Quick check: a formula
slides.body_md: Apply the method to calcium and phosphate.

visual.alt: Charges of calcium and phosphate

slides.narration: Calcium has valency two and phosphate has valency three. What is the formula of calcium phosphate?

slides.heading: Common factor and brackets
slides.body_md: Divide the subscripts by their **common factor** and put a **compound radical** in brackets only when it appears more than once.

visual.alt: Table showing common factors and brackets in three formulae

slides.narration: When both valencies are the same, the crossed numbers share a factor, so divide. Calcium carbonate becomes one calcium and one carbonate. A bracket is needed only when a group appears more than once, as in magnesium hydroxide. Sodium sulphate needs no bracket.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: ammonium phosphate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the formula of ammonium phosphate and count its atoms.

**Step 1.** Ammonium $\ce{NH4+}$ has valency 1; phosphate $\ce{PO4^3-}$ has valency 3.

**Step 2.** Cross over: $\ce{NH4}$ gets 3, $\ce{PO4}$ gets 1; bracket the ammonium: **(NH4)3PO4**.

**Step 3.** Atoms: N 3, H 12, P 1, O 4, total 20.

visual.alt: Table counting the atoms in ammonium phosphate

slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name $\ce{Fe2O3}$ and $\ce{Zn(NO3)2}$.

**Step 1.** In $\ce{Fe2O3}$, two Fe and three O: three O carry $3 \times 2 = 6$ negative charges, shared by two Fe, so each Fe is $6 \div 2 = 3$: iron(III) oxide.

**Step 2.** In $\ce{Zn(NO3)2}$ the radicals are zinc and nitrate: **zinc nitrate**.

slides.body_md: In sunlit, polluted air some molecules split into pieces with an **unpaired electron**. These **free radicals** are very reactive, and they are different from the charged radicals used in formulae.

sections.heading: 1. Symbols of elements
sections.body_md:
A **symbol** is a short sign, one capital letter or a capital followed by a small letter, that stands for an element.

| Element | Symbol | Element | Symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | H | Sodium (natrium) | Na |
| Carbon | C | Potassium (kalium) | K |
| Nitrogen | N | Iron (ferrum) | Fe |
| Oxygen | O | Copper (cuprum) | Cu |
| Sulphur | S | Silver (argentum) | Ag |
| Chlorine | Cl | Gold (aurum) | Au |
| Calcium | Ca | Lead (plumbum) | Pb |
| Zinc | Zn | Mercury (hydrargyrum) | Hg |

Some symbols come from the **Latin** names of the elements.

- **Qualitative meaning:** a symbol names the element.
- **Quantitative meaning:** a symbol stands for **one atom** of the element, and for its relative atomic mass (for example C: one atom of carbon, 12 u).

Cobalt is Co, but CO is the compound carbon monoxide: the second letter must be small.

key_terms.definition_md: A short sign, one or two letters, standing for an element and for one atom of it.

visual.alt: Table of four symbols taken from Latin names

sections.heading: 2. Valency
sections.body_md:
**Valency** is the combining power of an atom: the number of hydrogen atoms (or atoms that can replace hydrogen) that one atom combines with or displaces. Hydrogen has valency 1.

| Hydride | Valency of the other element |
|---|---|
| HCl | Chlorine 1 |
| H₂O | Oxygen 2 |
| NH₃ | Nitrogen 3 |
| CH₄ | Carbon 4 |

**Valence electrons** are the electrons in the outermost shell. They decide the valency.

- **Metals** lose their valence electrons: valency = number of valence electrons (1, 2 or 3).
- **Non-metals** gain electrons to complete the octet: valency = 8 − number of valence electrons (4 valence electrons gives valency 4).
- A full outer shell (a duplet in helium, an octet in neon and argon) means **valency 0**.

| Class | Valency | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Monovalent | 1 | Na, K, Cl |
| Divalent | 2 | Mg, Ca, O |
| Trivalent | 3 | Al, N, P |
| Tetravalent | 4 | C, Si |

Some metals have **variable valency**: iron is 2 in iron(II) and 3 in iron(III); copper is 1 or 2. The Roman number in the name gives the valency. Class IX only needs the common values.

key_terms.definition_md: The combining power of an atom, measured by the number of hydrogen atoms one atom combines with or replaces.

sections.heading: 3. Radicals
sections.body_md:
A **radical** is an atom or a group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as one unit in chemical reactions.

- **Positive (basic) radicals** are formed by metals, and also ammonium: sodium Na⁺, potassium K⁺, silver Ag⁺, **ammonium NH₄⁺**, magnesium Mg²⁺, calcium Ca²⁺, zinc Zn²⁺, copper(II) Cu²⁺, iron(II) Fe²⁺, lead(II) Pb²⁺, barium Ba²⁺, aluminium Al³⁺, iron(III) Fe³⁺.
- **Negative (acid) radicals** are formed by non-metals or groups with oxygen: chloride Cl⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, hydrogencarbonate HCO₃⁻, oxide O²⁻, sulphide S²⁻, sulphate SO₄²⁻, sulphite SO₃²⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, nitride N³⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻.
- A **simple radical** is a single charged atom (Na⁺, Cl⁻, O²⁻). A **compound radical** is a group of atoms with one charge (NH₄⁺, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻).
- The valency of an acid radical is the number of hydrogen ions the acid gives: $\ce{H2SO4 -> 2H+ + SO4^2-}$, so sulphate has valency 2.

Books differ on whether hydroxide is listed with the acid radicals; it is a negative radical, and here it is listed with them for convenience.

key_terms.definition_md: An atom or group of atoms with a charge that behaves as a single unit in reactions.
A group of atoms carrying one charge, such as sulphate or ammonium.

sections.heading: 4. Radicals in the atmosphere
sections.body_md:
This topic is about **free radicals** in the air, not the charged radicals of formulae.

- A **free radical** is a very reactive atom or fragment of a molecule with an **unpaired electron**. It forms when a bond breaks and each part keeps one electron, for example when sunlight breaks a chlorine molecule into two chlorine atoms.
- In polluted air, sunlight and heat act on vehicle and factory fumes and produce such radicals, which react at once with other molecules.

**Effects on living organisms**
- They irritate the eyes, nose, throat and lungs.
- They can damage cells and tissues in the body.
- They help form smog, and they harm plants and reduce crop growth.

**Ways to reduce them**
- Cut emissions from vehicles and industries; fit catalytic converters; use cleaner fuels.
- Stop burning rubbish, stubble and plastics in the open.
- Stop the use of chlorofluorocarbons; plant more trees.

Only the idea and the effects are asked at Class IX; the detailed reactions belong to higher classes.

key_terms.definition_md: A very reactive atom or fragment of a molecule that has an unpaired electron.

sections.heading: 5. Writing formulae and names
sections.body_md:
A compound is **neutral**, so the positive and negative charges cancel. The **criss-cross method** uses valencies to write the formula.

1. Write the positive radical first, then the negative one.
2. Write the valency of each above its symbol.
3. Cross over: the valency of one becomes the subscript of the other.
4. Divide both subscripts by their common factor; do not write a subscript of 1.
5. Put a **compound radical** in brackets if its subscript is more than 1.

| Compound | Working | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| Aluminium sulphate | Al 3, SO₄ 2 → Al₂(SO₄)₃ | **Al₂(SO₄)₃** |
| Calcium carbonate | Ca 2, CO₃ 2 → Ca₂(CO₃)₂ ÷ 2 | **CaCO₃** |
| Magnesium nitride | Mg 2, N 3 → Mg₃N₂ | **Mg₃N₂** |
| Ammonium sulphate | NH₄ 1, SO₄ 2 → (NH₄)₂SO₄ | **(NH₄)₂SO₄** |

**Naming:** the positive part first, then the negative part. One non-metal gets the ending **-ide** (chloride, oxide, sulphide, nitride). A group with oxygen keeps its name (sulphate, sulphite, nitrate, carbonate, phosphate). Variable valency goes in brackets: FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride, FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride. The valency of a metal can also be found back from a formula, for example in Fe₂O₃ three oxygen atoms carry 6 negative charges shared by two iron atoms.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing a symbol with two capitals (CL, NA) or two small letters.
- Taking the valency of nitrogen as 5 or of oxygen as 6 instead of 3 and 2.
- Changing the subscripts inside a radical (writing SO₃ for sulphate, or CaCO₂).
- Forgetting the common factor, or leaving a bracket round a radical that occurs once.
- Mixing up sulphate and sulphite, or nitrate and nitride.
- Giving the charged radicals of formulae when the question asks about free radicals in the air.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a symbol, a valency, a formula or a name.
- 2 marks: two matched points, or a formula with its working.
- 3 marks: three formulae or names, or three matched points on radicals in the air.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation with parts of 2 to 4 marks; give working for each formula.

cards.back_md: K, from kalium.

cards.front_md: Symbols of iron and copper, with Latin names?
cards.back_md: Fe (ferrum) and Cu (cuprum).

cards.front_md: Symbols of silver, gold, lead and mercury?
cards.back_md: Ag (argentum), Au (aurum), Pb (plumbum), Hg (hydrargyrum).

cards.front_md: Qualitative and quantitative meaning of a symbol?
cards.back_md: It names the element, and it stands for one atom of the element.

cards.front_md: Why is Co not the same as CO?
cards.back_md: Co is the element cobalt; CO is the compound carbon monoxide.

cards.front_md: What is valency?
cards.back_md: The combining power of an atom: the number of hydrogen atoms one atom combines with or replaces.

cards.front_md: Valency of the element in HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄?
cards.back_md: Chlorine 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3, carbon 4.

cards.front_md: What are valence electrons?
cards.back_md: The electrons in the outermost shell.

cards.front_md: Valency rule for a metal?
cards.back_md: Valency equals the number of valence electrons (1, 2 or 3).

cards.front_md: Valency rule for a non-metal?
cards.back_md: 8 minus the number of valence electrons.

cards.front_md: Valency of an element with electron arrangement 2, 8, 5?
Valency of a noble gas with a full outer shell?
cards.back_md: Zero.

cards.front_md: Name a monovalent, a divalent, a trivalent and a tetravalent element.
cards.back_md: Sodium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon.

cards.front_md: What does iron(III) mean?
cards.back_md: Iron with valency 3 (Fe³⁺).

cards.front_md: What is a radical?
cards.back_md: An atom or group of atoms with a charge that behaves as one unit in a reaction.

cards.front_md: Simple radical or compound radical: Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, Mg²⁺, NH₄⁺?
cards.back_md: Cl⁻ and Mg²⁺ are simple; NO₃⁻ and NH₄⁺ are compound.

cards.front_md: Name three compound negative radicals with valency 2.
cards.back_md: Sulphate, carbonate, sulphite.

cards.front_md: The one common positive compound radical?
cards.back_md: Ammonium, NH₄⁺.

cards.front_md: How does sulphuric acid show that sulphate has valency 2?
cards.back_md: H₂SO₄ gives two hydrogen ions and one sulphate radical.

cards.front_md: What is a free radical in the air?
cards.back_md: A very reactive atom or fragment of a molecule with an unpaired electron.

cards.front_md: Two harmful effects of free radicals in polluted air?
cards.back_md: They irritate the lungs and damage cells; they help form smog and harm plants.

cards.front_md: Two ways to reduce harmful radicals in the air?
cards.back_md: Cut vehicle and factory emissions; stop open burning (also plant trees, avoid CFCs).

cards.front_md: Criss-cross method in one line?
cards.back_md: The valency of one radical becomes the subscript of the other.

cards.front_md: Formula of aluminium sulphate?
cards.back_md: Al₂(SO₄)₃.

cards.front_md: Formula of calcium phosphate?
cards.back_md: Ca₃(PO₄)₂.

cards.front_md: When is a radical put in brackets?
cards.back_md: When it is a compound radical with a subscript above 1.

cards.front_md: Name FeCl₂ and FeCl₃.
cards.back_md: Iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: checking a formula
cards.back_md: Add the positive and negative charges: the total must be zero.

questions.stem_md: A label on a jar of metal pieces reads Pb. The element is
questions.solution_md: Pb comes from the Latin plumbum, which is lead, so option (c).

questions.stem_md: The formula of iron(III) hydroxide is
questions.solution_md: Iron(III) has valency 3 and hydroxide has valency 1, so hydroxide appears three times in brackets, option (c).

questions.stem_md: The compound (NH₄)₂SO₄ is named

questions.stem_md: Which pair gives an element and a symbol that comes from its Latin name?

questions.stem_md: A student writes CO as the symbol of the element cobalt. This is wrong because CO

options.text_md: is the formula of a compound of carbon and oxygen
is written with a small first letter

questions.stem_md: A jar in the school laboratory is marked N. State the qualitative and the quantitative meaning of this symbol.

answer.model_answer_md: **Qualitatively** N names the element **nitrogen**. **Quantitatively** it stands for **one atom** of nitrogen.

questions.stem_md: Copper wire is used in electrical cables. (a) Give the symbol of copper and the Latin word from which it is taken. (b) State what the symbol stands for quantitatively. (c) Write the symbols of gold and lead.

questions.solution_md: Six outer electrons mean two are needed to complete the octet: valency 8 − 6 = 2, a non-metal, option (c).

questions.solution_md: Two hydrogen atoms combine with one atom of Z, so its valency is 2; oxygen has valency 2, option (d).

questions.solution_md: The single outer electron is lost, valency 1, option (b).

options.text_md: P has valency 5 and Q has valency 7
P has valency 3 and Q has valency 1
P has valency 3 and Q has valency 7
P has valency 5 and Q has valency 1

questions.solution_md: P loses 3 electrons (valency 3); Q needs 8 − 7 = 1 more electron (valency 1), option (b).

options.text_md: The atom with the electron arrangement 2, 4
The atom with the electron arrangement 2, 8, 3
The atom with the electron arrangement 2, 6
The atom with the electron arrangement 2, 8, 5

questions.solution_md: Four outer electrons give valency 4. The others have valencies 3, 2 and 3, option (a).

options.text_md: is a non-metal in one of them
loses electrons in only one of them

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Magnesium has a valency of 2.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.stem_md: Write the electron arrangement and the valency of a calcium atom, which has 20 electrons.

answer.model_answer_md: Arrangement **2, 8, 8, 2**; valency **2**.

questions.stem_md: Name the hydride of each element and state its valency: (a) nitrogen (b) carbon.

questions.solution_md: Ammonia 3; methane 4.

questions.stem_md: An element Q has the electron arrangement 2, 8, 5. (a) What is meant by valency? (b) Find the valency of Q and say whether it is a metal or a non-metal. (c) Write the formula of its compound with hydrogen, using Q as its symbol.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Valency is the **combining power** of an atom, that is how many hydrogen atoms one atom can combine with.

**(b)** It needs three electrons to complete an octet, so valency is 8 − 5 = **3**; it is a **non-metal**.

**(c)** **QH₃**.

questions.solution_md: Combining power; 3, non-metal; QH₃.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The valency of every metal is equal to the number of electrons in its outer shell.
questions.solution_md: True for metals with one, two or three outer electrons, which lose them (the few with variable valency are exceptions).

questions.solution_md: Each of Zn²⁺, NH₄⁺ and Fe³⁺ carries a positive charge, option (a).

questions.solution_md: An atom with 8 electrons is oxygen; it gains 2 electrons to give 10 and becomes the oxide radical, option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hydroxide is a simple radical because it contains only one kind of charge.
questions.solution_md: False. Hydroxide, OH⁻, is a compound radical made of two atoms.

answer.model_answer_md: A **free radical**.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason why the free radicals in polluted air are not the same as the radicals Na⁺ and Cl⁻ written in formulae.

questions.solution_md: Unpaired electron against stable ions.

**Assertion (A):** Free radicals in polluted air have a complete outer shell of electrons.

**Reason (R):** Free radicals are very reactive.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A free radical has an unpaired electron, so (A) is false; (R) is true, option (b).

questions.stem_md: State two harmful effects of free radicals in polluted air on living organisms.

answer.model_answer_md: They **irritate the eyes and lungs** and **damage body cells**. (They also help form smog that harms plants.)

questions.solution_md: Irritation of eyes and lungs; cell damage.

questions.stem_md: Sunlight falls on air that is full of vehicle fumes. (a) State what happens to some molecules in the fumes. (b) Name the particles that form. (c) Suggest one way to reduce their formation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Bonds in the molecules **break**, each part keeping one electron.

questions.solution_md: Bonds break; free radicals; cut emissions.

questions.solution_md: Zn²⁺ and NO₃⁻ cross over to give Zn(NO₃)₂, option (c).

questions.solution_md: One Mg, two O and two H make 5 atoms, option (d).

questions.solution_md: X has valency 3 and Y has valency 2; crossing over gives X₂Y₃, option (c).

questions.solution_md: False. Aluminium has valency 3 and chlorine 1, so the formula is AlCl₃.

questions.solution_md: Potassium sulphide; iron(III) oxide.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the formula of calcium oxide is CaO and not Ca₂O₂.

answer.model_answer_md: Calcium and oxygen both have **valency 2**, so crossing over gives Ca₂O₂. The subscripts have the **common factor 2**, so they are divided to give the simplest formula **CaO**.

questions.solution_md: Equal valencies; subscripts divided by 2.

questions.stem_md: Write the formula of (a) barium sulphate, (b) silver sulphide and (c) iron(III) hydroxide, showing the valencies you used.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Ba 2, SO₄ 2: **BaSO₄** after dividing by 2.

**(b)** Ag 1, S 2: **Ag₂S**.

**(c)** Fe 3, OH 1: **Fe(OH)₃**.

questions.solution_md: BaSO₄; Ag₂S; Fe(OH)₃.

questions.stem_md: Show, step by step, how the criss-cross method gives the formula of magnesium phosphate.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Step 1.** Magnesium **Mg²⁺** has valency 2 and phosphate **PO₄³⁻** has valency 3.

**Step 2.** Cross over: Mg gets 3 and PO₄ gets 2, and there is no common factor.

**Step 3.** PO₄ is a compound radical used twice, so it goes in brackets: **Mg₃(PO₄)₂**.

questions.solution_md: Valencies 2 and 3; crossing; brackets.

questions.stem_md:
The diagram shows the criss-cross method for writing a formula. Its parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A, B, C, D and E. [5]

(b) State why no common factor had to be removed in this example. [1]

(c) Using the same method, write the formula of magnesium phosphate and name the two radicals in it. [2]

(d) Count the atoms of each element in one unit of the formula in the diagram. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is the symbol of the metal (calcium); **B** is its valency; **C** the crossing arrows; **D** the compound radical (phosphate); **E** the final formula.

**(b)** The valencies 2 and 3 have **no common factor** other than 1.

**(c)** **Mg₃(PO₄)₂**, from magnesium and phosphate radicals.

**(d)** Ca 3, P 2 and O 8, **13 atoms** in all.

questions.solution_md: Symbol, valency, arrows, radical, formula; 2 and 3 share no factor; Mg₃(PO₄)₂; 3 Ca, 2 P, 8 O.

questions.stem_md:
A school store has labels to be written for four salts made from these radicals: Zn²⁺, Fe³⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ and PO₄³⁻.

(a) Write the formulae of zinc nitrate, iron(III) sulphate, zinc phosphate and ammonium nitrate. [4]

(b) Which of the four formulae contains the largest number of atoms in one unit? Give that number. [2]

(c) Show, by adding charges, that the formula you wrote for iron(III) sulphate is electrically neutral. [2]

(d) Give two reasons why the name iron(III) sulphate carries the number III. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Zn(NO₃)₂**, **Fe₂(SO₄)₃**, **Zn₃(PO₄)₂**, **NH₄NO₃**.

**(b)** **Fe₂(SO₄)₃**, with **17 atoms** (2 Fe, 3 S, 12 O).

**(c)** Two Fe³⁺ give 2 × 3 = **+6**; three SO₄²⁻ give 3 × 2 = **−6**; the total is **zero**.

**(d)** Iron has **more than one valency** (2 and 3), so the number says **which one** is present, here valency 3.

questions.solution_md: Four formulae; Fe₂(SO₄)₃ with 17 atoms; +6 and −6; variable valency.

marking_scheme.step: Iron has more than one valency

questions.stem_md:
A student studies the elements fluorine, oxygen, nitrogen and carbon, which have 9, 8, 7 and 6 electrons in their atoms. Their hydrides are HF, H₂O, NH₃ and CH₄.

(a) Write the electron arrangement of each of the four elements. [4]

(b) State the valency of each element and show how it is connected to the number of outer electrons. [2]

(c) Write the formula of the compound of carbon with fluorine. [2]

(d) Explain why the valency rises from 1 to 4 as the outer electrons fall from 7 to 4. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** F **2, 7**; O **2, 6**; N **2, 5**; C **2, 4**.

**(b)** F **1**, O **2**, N **3**, C **4**. Each is **8 minus the outer electrons** (for carbon, equal to them).

**(c)** **CF4**.

**(d)** The fewer the electrons already in the outer shell, the **more electrons must be gained or shared** to reach eight, so the valency grows.

questions.solution_md: 2,7; 2,6; 2,5; 2,4; valencies 1 to 4; CF₄; octet argument.

questions.stem_md:
A town beside a busy highway has a brick kiln and a rubbish dump where waste is burnt in the open. On sunny afternoons residents complain of burning eyes and cough.

(a) Explain what a free radical is and how free radicals form in the air of this town. [3]

(b) State two harmful effects of these radicals on living organisms. [2]

(c) Suggest four steps the town can take to reduce the formation of harmful radicals. [4]

(d) State one difference between a free radical in the air and the sulphate radical in a formula. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A free radical is a **very reactive particle with an unpaired electron**. **Sunlight and heat break bonds** in pollutant molecules from fumes and smoke, and the pieces formed are radicals.

**(b)** They **irritate the eyes and lungs** and **damage body cells** (they also help form smog that harms plants).

**(c)** **Fit catalytic converters**, **cut kiln and vehicle emissions**, **stop open burning of waste**, and **plant trees** (or use cleaner fuels).

**(d)** A free radical has an **unpaired electron** and reacts at once; sulphate is a **stable charged group** of atoms.

questions.solution_md: Unpaired electron, bonds broken by sunlight; irritation and cell damage; four steps; unpaired electron versus stable group.

questions.stem_md:
A chemist's notebook lists these compounds by formula: K₂S, Cu(OH)₂, (NH₄)₂CO₃ and Fe(NO₃)₂.

(a) Name the four compounds. [4]

(b) For Cu(OH)₂, write the two radicals with their charges and show that the compound is neutral. [2]

(c) Write the formula of lead(II) chloride and give the number of atoms in one unit. [2]

(d) Sodium sulphite and sodium sulphate have different formulae although their radicals have the same valency. State how the formulae differ. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Potassium sulphide**; **copper(II) hydroxide**; **ammonium carbonate**; **iron(II) nitrate**.

**(b)** **Cu²⁺** and **OH⁻**: one Cu²⁺ gives +2 and two OH⁻ give −2, so the total is **zero**.

**(c)** **PbCl₂**, with **3 atoms** (1 Pb and 2 Cl).

**(d)** Sulphite is **SO₃²⁻** and sulphate is **SO₄²⁻**: the sulphate radical has **one more oxygen atom**, so the formulae are **Na₂SO₃** and **Na₂SO₄**.

questions.solution_md: Four names; Cu²⁺ and OH⁻ neutral; PbCl₂ with 3 atoms; sulphite has one oxygen fewer.

marking_scheme.step: One oxygen atom more in sulphate
